newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria c.bank to support lev where possible.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria c.bank to support lev where possible.

text.p: The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) will continue to support the lev on the local foreign exchange market as much as it can but cannot deplete reserves to counter a speculative dollar rush, BNB governor Lyubomir Filipov said.

"I would like to stress that we will continue to support the lev within the range of our capabilities and when we deem necessary," Filipov told national television, denying reports that the BNB would stop intervening altogether.

However, Filipov said it was natural for the BNB to abstain from large scale interventions at a time when billions of levs withdrawn from the State Savings Bank (SSB) in recent days were being poured onto the forex market.
"It is natural for the BNB whose reserves are relatively limited not to pour (foreign currency) to support speculative market sentiment (against the lev)," Filipov said.

A central bank official who asked not to be identified told Reuters on Wednesday that the bank planned to abstain from intervention and save its foreign exchange reserves for foreign debt payments and the possible introduction of a currency board system.

Filipov said the recent dollar rush on the cash forex market was caused by rumours that the finance ministry might suspend payments on government securities under a currency board system being discussed for Bulgaria.
The SSB is the country's largest savings institution. Some 75 percent of its deposits are invested in Treasury paper.
"These are ill-intentioned rumours, that the SSB faces problems," said Filipov.
Individuals have withdrawn some 13 billion levs from the SSB since the middle of last week until Tuesday, part of which were converted in foreign currency, SSB head Bistra Dimitrova told Reuters.

Asked whether the lev decline was due just to panic among depositors triggered by comments from banking officials, Filipov said that there were also fundamental reasons for the depreciation of the national currency.
"I told parliament that Bulgaria has to service foreign debt payments of some $1 billion a year while its trade surplus rarely can top $300-400 million a year," Filipov said.
"We need a capital inflow from abroad."

Payments of $300 million on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt fall due in the first quarter of 1997 and debt markets speculate that Bulgaria could become the first country to default on a Brady debt restructuring deal.
BNB foreign exchange reserves reserves stood near $541 million at the end of October, down from $1.434 billion a year ago. The central bank also manages gold reserves worth some $400 million.
